transcript:
This message comes from Google Workspace with Gemini.
One subscription that does it all.
Personalized AI and premium business versions of Gmail, Google Docs, Drive, and more.
Try it free for 14 days at goo.gle/workspace with Gemini.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
A federal judge has extended an order for now,
blocking the Trump administration from banning reporters from CNN,
MS Now, and Politico from the White House.
The U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban
violates the journalists' constitutional rights to free speech and due process.
Kelly said that the news outlets are likely to succeed in their case against the president.
Democratic and Republican party leaders have been in a legal battle about ad rates
since earlier this year.
Today, the Supreme Court again sided with the Republicans, at least for now,
and Pierre's Mahom Javed has more.
The GOP has been given another win in the ongoing ad rate dispute between the two parties.
A recent Federal Communications Commission policy gives party committees discounted ad rates,
previously only offered to candidates.
Democratic leaders, including former Senator Sherrod Brown, challenged this policy,
and a lower court ordered the FCC to finalize its new rule before the November 3rd elections.
Now, the Supreme Court has intervened,
saying the FCC does not have to follow that deadline.
This means both party committees can continue to enjoy discounted ad rates for the upcoming midterm,
and the Republican Party Committee has considerably more in its coffers
than its Democratic counterpart, Mahom Javed, NPR News.
The Justice Department is threatening California with possible legal action over
what it says are non-citizens who received mail ballots for next month's midterm elections.
A letter sent to the Secretary of State gives California 48 hours
to determine whether any non-citizens are listed.
Streaming giant Netflix is laying off 6% of its staff amid growing competition,
and Pierre's Montelite-Albarco reports it's the biggest round of layoffs in four years.
Netflix staffers around the world got the news today that a thousand of them are losing their jobs.
In an email memo to employees, co-ceos Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos wrote
that most of the cuts would be in Netflix's product, tech, legal, and HR teams.
With increased competition and slower growth,
the streamer has been trying to get subscribers to spend more time on its platform
by adding live sports and events, video podcasts, and shows by YouTube creators.
Netflix joins other tech and media companies with recent layoffs, including Amazon and Disney,
and the new Skydance merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. is expected to result in job cuts soon.
Montelite-Albarco, NPR News, Los Angeles.
The Social Security Administration projects a 3.6% cost of living increase
on checks for older adults and people with disabilities starting in 2027.
Some recipients say it won't offset rising prices.
This adjustment means 75 extra dollars per month for the nearly 72 million Social Security
beneficiaries and about 7.3 million supplemental security income recipients.
Meanwhile, inflation continues to pressure household budgets and savings.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Supermarkets in France and the Netherlands are dealing with the aftermath of a cyber attack
that disrupted refrigeration systems.
The attack caused temperatures to soar, leading to significant food losses.
Investigations are underway, but no perpetrators have been identified.
Experts say the attack highlights vulnerabilities
and the need for better cybersecurity measures.
A parrot has filed a class-action lawsuit against OpenAI for allowing her teenage
children to use chat GPT without parental consent and profiting off their data.
NPR's Ho Jing Nan has more.
The lawsuit filed in California alleges that OpenAI allowed the plaintiff's children
to bypass its parental consent requirement easily, and that the chatbot continued to
engage with one of the children even after the girl said that she was 12,
below the minimum user age that OpenAI laid out in its own policy.
According to the complaint, the children shared intimate life details with the chatbot,
including selfies, their anxieties about their appearance, and a photo of insects in the bathroom.
The plaintiff alleges that OpenAI unjustly profits off of such user data
and demands compensation from the company.
In response to NPR, OpenAI says it strongly disagrees with its "misguided lawsuit."
It says it requires parental consent for underage users
and lets teen users opt out of letting OpenAI train on their data.
Ho Jing Nan, NPR News.
Americans have a new sunscreen option for the first time in over 25 years.
The FDA approved the chemical ingredient BEMT back in June.
The ingredient is already popular in Europe and is supposed to offer
broad protection without the cosmetic downsides of older ingredients.
This is NPR News.
This message comes from Angie.
Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years.
For everything from minor repairs to major remodels,
find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
